title: Count the words, then the pairs
prompt:
A model can only read numbers, so the shop's repair notes need turning into counts. Write three functions: `tokens` cuts a note into clean lowercase words, `bag` counts each word, and `pairs` counts each pair of words that sit side by side.

When it works, `python3 wordcount.py` shows that the pair `('the', 'lamp')` appears twice.
hints: `text.lower().split()` gives lowercase words with the punctuation still attached. `word.strip(".,!?")` takes it off the ends.
In `bag`, start every new word at 0 with `counts.get(w, 0)` and add 1. In `pairs`, `zip(words, words[1:])` lines each word up with the next one.
`for first, second in zip(words, words[1:]):` then `counts[(first, second)] = counts.get((first, second), 0) + 1`.
explain_after: Word counts are one simple way to turn text into numbers; scikit-learn's `MultinomialNB`, a classic text classifier, takes exactly this kind of word-count vector as input [ml-079]. Counting pairs is the first step toward an n-gram model, which guesses a word from only the last few words before it [ml-088].
